You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

=== TEXT A ===
# Why Most Product Roadmaps Fail

Every product organization builds roadmaps, yet most end up abandoned, ignored, or quietly rewritten into irrelevance. The failure is rarely about effort or intelligence. It is structural: roadmaps are asked to be a plan, a promise, and a persuasion tool at once — and those roles conflict.

First, most roadmaps confuse outputs with outcomes. They are lists of features with dates attached — "launch X in Q2" — with the "why" missing. Which customer problem does X solve? Which metric will it move? Without stated outcomes, teams become feature factories, optimizing for shipping rather than value, and the roadmap can only be judged by whether things shipped on time, not whether they mattered.

Second, they offer false precision. Attaching dates to unexplored work implies a certainty that product development never has. Building software is an exercise in learning, and learning resists scheduling. When reality diverges — an assumption fails, discovery reveals a better solution, a dependency slips — the dated roadmap becomes a ledger of broken promises rather than a planning tool. The dates convert hypotheses into commitments.

Third, many roadmaps are political artifacts rather than strategic ones. They emerge from negotiation among stakeholders: sales needs a feature to close a deal, an executive wants a box checked from the vision deck, engineering lobbies for debt paydown. The result is a compromise that satisfies everyone individually and serves the customer not at all. Evidence — usage data, customer interviews, market signals — is conspicuously absent from the process.

Fourth, a single roadmap cannot serve every audience. Leadership wants strategy; sales wants something sellable; engineering wants a plan; customers want commitments. Pressed into all these roles, the document fails at each. The most damaging version is when sales treats the roadmap as a catalog and sells future features to customers, at which point flexibility dies. The roadmap is now a contract, and every reprioritization is a breach.

What would a better roadmap look like? It would express problems and goals rather than solutions: "reduce onboarding drop-off," not "launch onboarding wizard." It would use horizons — now, next, later — instead of dates, staying honest about uncertainty. It would be a living document, revised as learning accumulates rather than defended as it ages. And it would distinguish clearly between what is committed and what is merely being explored.

The deepest issue is that most organizations treat the roadmap as a promise to keep when it should be a hypothesis to test. Plans fail when they pretend the future is known. Roadmaps survive only when they admit what they are: a statement of direction, grounded in evidence, flexible enough to change when the world does. The roadmap doesn't fail because plans changed; it fails because it pretended they wouldn't.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
# Why Most Product Roadmaps Fail

Most product roadmaps fail not because teams lack ambition, intelligence, or effort, but because roadmaps are often mistaken for plans rather than treated as hypotheses. They present a confident sequence of features months or years into the future, even though customer needs, market conditions, technology, and business priorities are constantly changing.

A common failure begins with confusing outputs with outcomes. Roadmaps frequently list features—“launch dashboard,” “add integrations,” or “redesign onboarding”—without explaining what problem each initiative solves or how success will be measured. As a result, teams become busy delivering functionality rather than creating value. A feature can be completed on time and still fail to improve retention, revenue, satisfaction, or efficiency.

Roadmaps also fail when they are built around unrealistic certainty. Dates are often treated as commitments before the team understands the complexity of the work. Dependencies, technical debt, research, approvals, and unexpected discoveries are underestimated or ignored. Once deadlines are published, however, they become politically difficult to change. Teams then rush, reduce quality, or deliver compromises simply to preserve the appearance of predictability.

Another problem is that roadmaps are frequently shaped by the loudest stakeholders. Sales requests, executive preferences, competitor activity, and individual customer demands can all influence priorities. These inputs may be valuable, but without a consistent decision-making framework they produce a disconnected collection of initiatives. The roadmap becomes a negotiation artifact rather than a coherent strategy.

Poor communication makes the problem worse. Some roadmaps are too vague to guide teams; others are so detailed that they create rigidity. Internal teams may interpret them as promises, while customers may interpret them as guarantees. When assumptions change, leaders may quietly shift priorities without explaining why, damaging trust and creating confusion.

Finally, many organizations fail to learn from their roadmaps. They track whether projects were delivered, but not whether the intended outcomes occurred. Without reviewing results, teams cannot distinguish effective decisions from expensive mistakes. The roadmap becomes an annual ritual instead of a feedback loop.

A better roadmap communicates direction, priorities, and reasoning rather than pretending to predict the future. It focuses on customer and business outcomes, uses time horizons appropriate to the level of uncertainty, and makes assumptions visible. Near-term work can be more specific, while distant priorities remain flexible. Most importantly, progress should be evaluated by impact, not activity.

Product roadmaps fail when they promise certainty in an uncertain environment. They succeed when they align people around problems worth solving, establish clear measures of progress, and remain adaptable as evidence changes.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}
